body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Weekly web-based symptom reporting during outpatient chemotherapy and emergency department visits: a randomised trial","authors":"Halvorsen-Mbatha K, Duarte-Whitfield R, Oyelaran-Szabo T","year":2017,"venue":"Journal of Supportive Oncology Practice","doi":"10.5555/jsop.2017.0231","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 612 adults starting outpatient chemotherapy at two centres to weekly web-based symptom reporting with nurse alerts or to usual care, in which patients telephoned the unit when concerned. Over six months, 34 percent of patients in the reporting group and 41 percent in the usual care group had at least one emergency department visit. Health-related quality of life declined less in the reporting group. Completion of expected weekly reports was 83 percent in the first month and 71 percent by month six. Patients over 75 and those without home internet access were underrepresented, and both centres had a dedicated nurse reading alerts."},{"title":"Completion of weekly electronic symptom reports after routine rollout in a comprehensive cancer centre","authors":"Sorensen-Adeyemi L, Tan-Holbrook G","year":2022,"venue":"Oncology Nursing Informatics","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We describe completion of weekly electronic symptom reports in the first year after routine rollout to 1,480 patients receiving chemotherapy. Completion of expected reports was 78 percent in the first month of treatment and 46 percent by month six. Completion was lower in patients aged 75 or over (odds ratio 0.52) and in those living in the most deprived areas (odds ratio 0.61). Patients who received a nurse call after their first severe alert completed more of their later reports. The study could not tell whether falling completion reflected improving symptoms or disengagement from the programme."},{"title":"Why patients stop reporting symptoms electronically during chemotherapy: an interview study","authors":"Nkemelu-Varga A, Pereira-Lindholm C, Watanabe-Osei J","year":2021,"venue":"Cancer Care Experience","doi":"10.5555/cce.2021.0109","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 31 adults who had stopped weekly electronic symptom reporting before finishing chemotherapy. Three reasons recurred: feeling that nobody read the answers, questions that did not fit their symptoms, and difficulty with the tablet or phone. Several participants said that they stopped after reporting a severe symptom and receiving no call within the day. Participants valued a named nurse and the option of reporting on paper. Interviews were held at one urban centre, and most participants spoke the majority language, so the views of patients who needed an interpreter are missing."},{"title":"Alert burden and response times after introducing electronic symptom monitoring in a chemotherapy day unit","authors":"Gallagher-Otieno F, Brandt-Moreau S","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Oncology Nursing Operations","doi":"10.5555/jono.2023.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We measured alert volume and nurse response time for 12 months after a chemotherapy day unit introduced weekly electronic symptom reports. The unit received a median of 38 severe-symptom alerts per week. The median time from alert to nurse contact was 3.1 hours on weekdays and 19.5 hours at weekends, when no triage nurse was rostered to read alerts. Nurses reported that 29 percent of alerts concerned symptoms already known to the team. The unit added a weekend review rota in month nine, and the evaluation ended before its effect could be measured."},{"title":"Electronic patient-reported outcome monitoring during systemic cancer treatment: a systematic review of randomised trials","authors":"Achterberg-Kimura E, Fitzgerald-Nwosu P, Lemaire-Castellano D","year":2020,"venue":"Supportive Care Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/scer.2020.0418","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four databases to 2019 for randomised trials of electronic symptom monitoring during chemotherapy or immunotherapy. In all, 14 trials with 5,210 patients met the inclusion criteria. Emergency department visits were reduced in 6 of the 9 trials that measured them, and quality of life favoured monitoring in 8 of 11. Effects on survival were reported in two trials. Adherence to reporting was described inconsistently, and no trial reported outcomes separately for patients who stopped reporting. Risk of bias was moderate to high because neither patients nor staff could be blinded."},{"title":"Tablet versus paper symptom questionnaires among adults aged 75 and over receiving chemotherapy: a cross-sectional comparison","authors":"Moreno-Achebe I, Lindqvist-Rao H","year":2016,"venue":"Geriatric Oncology Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We offered 204 adults aged 75 and over receiving chemotherapy a symptom questionnaire either on paper or on a tablet at the same clinic visit. In all, 57 percent chose paper. Those who chose the tablet completed it in a median of 6 minutes and those who chose paper in 4 minutes. Among tablet users, 18 percent needed help from staff to finish. Choosing paper was associated with living alone and with having no internet access at home. The authors recommend keeping a paper route whenever electronic reporting is introduced for older adults."},{"title":"Integrating completion data and patient interviews to evaluate electronic symptom reporting: a mixed methods evaluation in a regional cancer network","authors":"Okafor-Lindgren B, Castaneda-Hughes M, Yilmaz-Fraser D","year":2024,"venue":"Implementation in Cancer Care","doi":"10.5555/icc.2024.0062","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We combined 12 months of report completion data from three regional centres with interviews with 24 patients and 11 nurses, and integrated the two strands in a joint display. Completion fell most steeply after the first missed nurse response to a severe alert. Interviews explained the pattern: patients read an unanswered alert as a sign that reporting did not matter. Centres that introduced a same-day response standard recovered completion within three months. The evaluation was not designed to estimate effects on emergency visits, and the centres chose themselves to take part."}]}
